sections.h: The call and the first oracles (chapters 1-6)
sections.b:
Jeremiah is called in 627 BC, in Josiah's thirteenth year, while he is still 'a boy' (1:2, 6). The LORD says he knew him and set him apart before he was born, puts his words in his mouth and gives him six verbs for his work: to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant (1:5-10). Two visions, an almond branch and a boiling pot, give him the message in advance: the LORD is watching over his word, and disaster will come from the north (1:11-16).

Chapters 2-6 are poems of accusation and alarm: Israel the bride who forgot (2), the sisters Israel and Judah and the call to turn back (3:1-4:4), the ram's horn and the undoing of creation (4:5-31), the search for one honest person (5), and the siege poems that end with the verdict 'rejected silver' (6).

sections.h: Prophecy as the LORD's word in a prophet's mouth
sections.b: Jeremiah's call shows what a prophet is in the Bible's own terms: not a seer of the future first of all, but a messenger who delivers the words the LORD puts in his mouth (1:9). The language echoes the promise of a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:18). The prophet is called before birth, sent to people who will not listen, and promised protection but not success (1:8, 19). His words are 'fire' (5:14) and he is a 'tester' of his people (6:27).

sections.h: 'Peace, peace' when there is no peace
sections.b: Jeremiah's first charge against the prophets of his day is that they say what the people want to hear. They cry 'Peace, peace' and say the nation's broken place is healed, 'as though it were a trifle' (6:14). He charges that 'the prophets prophesy by a lie' and the priests 'rule at their side', and that the people love it (5:31); that they speak 'wind' without the LORD's word (5:13); and that from prophet to priest all deal in lies (6:13). The test he gives later is whether they have stood in the LORD's council (23:18, 22) and whether their word comes true (Deuteronomy 18:21-22; Jeremiah 28:9).

sections.b: Jeremiah's call is dated to Josiah's thirteenth year (627 BC) and the 'sisters' message of 3:6-4:2 to Josiah's reign (3:6). Josiah's reform of 622 BC (2 Kings 22-23) is not mentioned by name in these chapters. Jeremiah's verdict on the repentance of Judah, that it returned to the LORD 'not with her whole heart, but with a lie' (3:10), is often read as a comment on how far the reform went.

sections.h: The foe from the north in Jeremiah 1-6
sections.b: Chapters 1-6 return to a 'foe from the north' (1:13-15; 4:6; 5:15-17; 6:1, 22-26), a lion that destroys nations and an army with a strange language. The poems do not name it. Scholars have identified it with the Scythians (Herodotus 1.103-106), with Babylon after its rise, or as a traditional picture of chaos from the north (Childs). Later chapters name Babylon and Nebuchadnezzar (21:2; 25:9), and 6:22-24 is reused against Babylon herself in 50:41-43.

sections.b: Chapter 2 portrays idolatry as leaving a spring of living water for cracked cisterns (2:13), as a vine gone bad (2:21), and as a prostitute sprawled under every green tree (2:20). The people call a piece of wood 'my father' and a stone 'you gave birth to us' (2:27), and have as many gods as cities (2:28). Idols are 'empty things' (hevel, 2:5) and those who follow them become empty. The 'Shameful Thing' of 3:24 is Baal.

Jeremiah speaks of 'the Baals' (2:23), the local forms of the Canaanite storm god who was thought to give rain and fertility. The prophets of the day 'prophesied by Baal' (2:8), and the drought of the next chapters tests who really gives rain (compare 5:24). Jeremiah also calls Baal bosheth, 'the Shameful Thing', that has eaten up the ancestors' labor and children (3:24), a substitute for his name, as in Ish-bosheth. The LORD is Israel's real ba'al, 'husband' (3:14).

sections.h: Shuv: turning back and turning away
sections.b: The great repentance passage of the Old Testament is Jeremiah 3:1-4:4, built on the Hebrew root shuv ('turn, return'). Israel is 'the one who turned away' (meshuvah), and the LORD says, 'Turn back, you who turned away' (3:12; 3:14, 22). The turning is a matter of admitting guilt (3:13), of an honest confession (3:22-25) and of removing the detestable things and swearing truly (4:1-2). It must reach the heart: 'Be circumcised for the LORD' (4:4).

Jeremiah 5:19 gives the answer to the question the exiles would ask: 'For what reason did the LORD our God do all this to us?' The answer is a rule that fits the crime: because they served foreign gods in their own land, they will serve outsiders in a land that is not theirs. The pattern is the same as in Deuteronomy 29:24-28; 1 Kings 9:8-9; Jeremiah 16:10-13 and 22:8-9.

In chapter 2 the people go to Egypt and Assyria 'to drink the water of the Shihor' and 'of the River' (2:18); men from Memphis and Tahpanhes will crush their skulls (2:16); and they will be shamed by Egypt as they were by Assyria (2:36). Jeremiah later warns against alliance with Egypt against Babylon (37:5-10), and takes the last Judeans to Tahpanhes (43:7).

sections.h: The circumcision of the heart and ears
sections.b: Jeremiah 4:4 calls on Judah to 'be circumcised for the LORD' and to remove 'the foreskins of your hearts', repeating Deuteronomy 10:16 and 30:6. In 6:10 their ears are 'uncircumcised' and cannot listen. In 9:25-26 Jeremiah says that all the nations that practice circumcision, Israel among them, are uncircumcised in heart. The New Testament takes up the language of Romans 2:28-29, Colossians 2:11 and Acts 7:51.

sections.b: In four visionary lines Jeremiah sees the earth 'shapeless and empty' (the words of Genesis 1:2), the heavens without light, the mountains quaking, no human being, the birds gone and the orchard land a wilderness (4:23-26). The poem takes the order of creation apart. It joins Isaiah 24, Zephaniah 1:2-3 and Hosea 4:3. The same chapter says that the land will be a desolation, but the LORD will not make a complete end (4:27). In 5:22 the sea keeps to its decreed limit.

sections.h: The search for one just person and the orphan's case
sections.b: The LORD tells Jeremiah to search the streets of Jerusalem for one person 'who acts with justice and looks for faithfulness'. If there is one, he will forgive the city (5:1). The rich grow 'fat and glossy' and do not plead the case of the orphan or judge the rights of the poor (5:28). Jeremiah says later that doing justice for the poor and needy is what it means to know the LORD (22:15-16).

sections.h: Offerings the LORD does not accept (6:20)
sections.b: 'Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba ... Your burnt offerings cannot be accepted' (6:20). The offerings named were lawful (Leviticus 2:1-2; Exodus 30:23), and they are rejected because the worshipers refuse the LORD's words and his teaching and oppress one another (6:6-7, 19). It is the same message as Isaiah 1:11-17, Amos 5:21-24, Hosea 6:6 and Micah 6:6-8. Jeremiah 7:21-23 goes further.

The refrain 'I will not make a complete end' appears in 4:27, 5:10 and 5:18 (and later in 30:11 and 46:28). It limits the judgment: the LORD will not wipe out his people. The remnant is gleaned like the last grapes of a vine (6:9); the people are tested like silver, and in the end found to be 'rejected silver' (6:30), yet the refining is meant to leave something (compare Isaiah 1:25; Zechariah 13:9).

sections.h: The ark that will not be missed (3:16)
sections.b: Jeremiah 3:16 says that in the days of renewal people will no longer say 'The ark of the covenant of the LORD'; it will not come to mind, be missed or be made again. Jerusalem itself will be called the LORD's throne (3:17). The fate of the ark is not told in the Bible. 2 Maccabees 2:4-8 says Jeremiah hid it on Mount Nebo; the Talmud says Josiah hid it (Yoma 52b); the Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that it is in Aksum.

'Take your stand on the roads and look. Ask about the paths of long ago: where is the road that is good? Walk on it, and you will find rest' (6:16). The offer of a good road and a refusal ('We will not walk on it') is the same choice as Deuteronomy 30:15-20 and Psalm 1. Jesus' invitation, 'you will find rest for your souls' (Matthew 11:29), uses the wording of the Hebrew of this verse.

Jeremiah 3:1 asks, on the basis of Deuteronomy 24:1-4, whether a man can take back a wife he has divorced after she has belonged to another. The law says he cannot; the LORD says to Israel, who has had many lovers, 'Yet return to me'. Israel and Judah are pictured as two sisters, one divorced (3:8) and one still unfaithful. The picture of marriage and divorce as the covenant is Hosea's and Ezekiel's too.

sections.h: The loyal love of Israel's youth (2:2)
sections.b: Usually hesed is the LORD's loyal love for his people. In Jeremiah 2:2 the LORD remembers Israel's hesed: 'the loyal love of your youth, the love of your engagement', when she followed him in the wilderness. In 3:12 the LORD calls himself hasid, 'loyal', and will not hold a grudge forever.

The LORD planted Israel as a choice vine, 'all of it seed that could be trusted', and it turned into 'the spoiled shoots of a foreign vine' (2:21). The picture of Israel as the LORD's vine is also in Psalm 80:8-16, Isaiah 5:1-7, Hosea 10:1 and Ezekiel 15; Jesus calls himself 'the true vine' (John 15:1).

The people 'have traded their Glory for something that cannot help' (2:11); Psalm 106:20 says the same, and Paul takes it up in Romans 1:23. A Jewish tradition lists the verse among the scribes' corrections (tiqqune soferim), where the original is said to be 'my Glory'.

'My innards, my innards! I am writhing' (4:19) is the first of Jeremiah's personal laments. The speaker may be the prophet, or the prophet giving voice to God's pain. It begins a series that includes 8:18-9:3, 10:19-20, 14:17-18 and the confessions of 11-20.

In 4:28 the LORD says of the coming judgment: 'I have spoken, I have planned it, and I have not changed my mind, and I will not turn back from it.' Elsewhere in the book God may change his mind if the people turn (18:7-10; 26:3, 13), and he says he is 'tired of relenting' (15:6). Readers have reconciled these as the difference between a warning that is conditional and a sentence once the time for turning is past.

sections.h: Jerusalem as the city that does not know
sections.b: Jerusalem is the city whose streets contain no one who acts with justice (5:1), the pasture that shepherds will besiege (6:2-3), the city that 'must be called to account' because 'it is nothing but oppression all through' (6:6), and also the throne of the LORD for all nations in the age to come (3:17).

Jeremiah's Daughter Zion is a woman in labor, gasping and stretching out her hands (4:31), a dainty pasture (6:2), and the target of a cruel army (6:23). The title is common to Isaiah, Micah and Lamentations.

The city dresses in scarlet and jewels for lovers who 'reject' her and 'want your life' (4:30); the lovers are her allies, Egypt and Assyria first (2:18, 36), and later Babylon. The prophets Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel use the picture of a woman's lovers for political alliances.

Ancient war began with rites that made it holy. In 6:4 the attackers say 'Consecrate war against her!' and they are the LORD's instrument: 'Chop down the trees and pile up an assault ramp' (6:6). Other prophets speak of foreign armies as the LORD's 'consecrated ones' (Isaiah 13:3; Jeremiah 51:27-28).

sections.h: 'The LORD says this' and 'the LORD declares'
sections.b: Jeremiah's messages open with koh amar YHWH, 'The LORD says this' (2:2), the messenger's formula, and close with ne'um YHWH, 'the LORD declares' (1:8). The name of the God of Armies is used with it (2:19). The Greek often says 'Lord' or 'Almighty' instead.
'I have set my words in your mouth' (1:9) echoes the promise of a prophet like Moses in Deuteronomy 18:18. Rashi connects the two: each prophesied for forty years.

Jeremiah 2:8 charges the priests, those 'who held the law in their hands', with not knowing the LORD; compare 8:8 and 6:19, where the LORD's 'teaching' is rejected. The charge is that the guardians of the Torah did not live it.

If Israel turns back and swears truly, 'the nations will bless themselves by him' (4:2), in the language of the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3; 22:18; 26:4). The blessing of the nations depends here on Israel's repentance.
